opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to frame it is that there are two exponentials happening at once, and people tend to conflate them. One is the capability exponential: the models keep getting smarter, more reliable, and able to do longer and more autonomous tasks. The other is the diffusion exponential: how fast that capability actually gets absorbed into the economy. The second one is fast, faster than almost any previous technology, but it's not infinitely fast, and I think a lot of the confusion comes from people expecting the two curves to be the same.

When you look at our revenue growth, a lot of it so far has been concentrated in places where adoption is unusually frictionless. Coding is the clearest example. Developers are early adopters by temperament. The feedback loop is tight: you write code, you run it, it works or it doesn't. And the person choosing the tool is often the person using it, so there's no long procurement cycle. That's why you've seen coding take off so dramatically, both for us and across the industry.

Then there's a second wave, which I think we're in the middle of now: large enterprises in finance, pharma, insurance, legal, customer service, places where the value is enormous but the adoption process looks very different. You have compliance reviews, security reviews, integration with legacy systems, change management, retraining people, figuring out who's accountable when the model makes a mistake. None of that is a capability problem. The model might already be good enough to do the task, and it still takes a year or two for an organization to actually rewire itself around it. So I expect enterprise adoption to keep growing very fast, but in a lumpier way, where a company pilots something, it works, and then suddenly it's deployed across tens of thousands of employees.

The third wave, which is further out but which I think about a lot, is when the models are capable enough to act more like autonomous agents, or what I've called a country of geniuses in a data center. At that point the bottleneck shifts. It's less about whether the model can help a human do their job and more about the physical and institutional world keeping up. You can have a model that designs a drug candidate in a day, but clinical trials still take time, manufacturing still takes time, regulators still need to be convinced. So you get enormous acceleration in some places and real friction in others.

My overall expectation is that this spreads faster than skeptics think and slower than the most enthusiastic people in the Bay Area think. Faster because the products are easy to try, the value is obvious once people use them, and there's competitive pressure: if your competitor is using AI to move twice as fast, you can't sit it out. Slower because organizations are made of people, processes, and laws, and those don't change at the speed of a model release.

And I'd add one caveat about revenue specifically. Revenue is a lagging and imperfect indicator. It tells you where people are willing to pay today, which is useful, but the bigger economic effects, things like productivity growth across whole sectors, or changes in what jobs look like, will show up more gradually and in ways that are harder to measure. That's part of why we try to study this directly, looking at how people are actually using the models, because I think it's important for policymakers and the public to see the transition while it's happening rather than after the fact.

r001.rationale: It says enterprise adoption faces compliance, security, integration, and change-management work, and that even when the model is already capable, rewiring an organization can take a year or two.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes the “capability exponential” from the “diffusion exponential,” describing model improvement separately from how quickly capability is absorbed into the economy.

r003.rationale: It describes diffusion as “faster than almost any previous technology.”

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it's going to be uneven, and that's actually the most important thing to understand about it.

If you look at our revenue growth, the thing that strikes me is that it's not spreading smoothly across every sector at once. It's spreading from the inside out, starting with the people who are closest to the technology. So coding was first, and that's not a coincidence. Software engineers are the people who can most easily recognize when the model is good, they can verify the output, and the output is text that plugs directly into their existing workflow. So you get this very fast adoption curve there, and that's what's driven a lot of our numbers.

Then I think what happens is you get these concentric rings. The next ring is things that look like coding even if they're not called coding. Data analysis, financial modeling, legal document review, scientific literature synthesis. Work where there's a lot of structured text, where the output can be checked, and where the people doing it have some tolerance for a tool that's ninety-five percent right and needs a human looking over its shoulder.

And then beyond that you get into the parts of the economy that are much slower to move, and I think people underestimate how slow. Healthcare, government, heavily regulated industries, physical industries. Not because the models can't help there, they can, but because the bottleneck isn't model capability. The bottleneck is integration, trust, liability, regulation, and frankly just organizational inertia. A hospital doesn't change how it operates because a model got better. It changes when someone builds a product, gets it through procurement, gets it through compliance, and retrains the staff. That takes years.

So I'd actually push back a little on the framing that rapid revenue growth tells you adoption is going to be fast everywhere. What I think it tells you is that where the friction is low, adoption is extremely fast, faster than almost any technology we've seen. And that creates a kind of gap. You'll have some parts of the economy that have been transformed, and other parts that look almost unchanged, and that gap is going to persist for a while.

I actually think that gap is the thing to worry about more than the pace itself. If the models keep improving the way I expect them to, you're going to have capabilities that could in principle do a huge fraction of cognitive work, and a diffusion process that's much slower and much more lumpy than the capability curve. And the economic and social consequences come from that mismatch, not from either curve on its own.

The other thing I'd say is that I don't think the right mental model is "AI as a tool that gets adopted." I think for a lot of the economy it's going to end up looking more like "AI as a new kind of labor," where the question isn't whether a company buys a license, it's whether they restructure around having a large number of very capable agents working alongside their people. And that's a much bigger organizational change. Companies that figure out how to do that are going to pull away from companies that don't, and that's part of why I think the diffusion will be unequal even within sectors, not just across them.

r001.rationale: It says adoption in healthcare and other sectors is delayed by integration, trust, liability, regulation, procurement, compliance, and staff retraining, even when models can help.

r002.rationale: It contrasts rapidly improving model capabilities with a slower, uneven diffusion process through the economy.

r003.rationale: It says adoption can be faster than almost any technology where friction is low, but does not predict that diffusion across the economy overall will be much faster than previous technologies; it emphasizes that diffusion will be slow and uneven in many sectors.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to be uneven. Revenue can grow very quickly while adoption across the economy is still at an early stage. Those aren’t contradictory: you can have enormous demand in a few areas where the technology is already useful, while other areas take much longer to change.

Coding is a good example of where you’d expect adoption to move quickly. People are already working in a digital environment, they can try the model easily, and they can often check whether the output works. In other settings, you have to connect the model to internal systems, figure out how to evaluate it, and change the way people work. That takes time even if the underlying model is capable.

So I’d distinguish the improvement in the technology from the speed at which organizations can absorb it. They affect each other, but they’re different processes. Our revenue growth tells you that there’s substantial demand for what these systems can do today. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you how quickly every industry will adopt them.

The interesting question is whether AI can help remove some of those adoption bottlenecks—whether it can help with the integration and evaluation work itself. If it can, then diffusion could accelerate. But I’d still expect a pattern where some tasks change very quickly, and other parts of the economy lag behind.

r001.rationale: It says organizations must connect models to internal systems, evaluate them, and change workflows, which takes time even when the model is capable.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes improvement in the technology from how quickly organizations absorb it and AI diffuses.

r003.rationale: It says diffusion could accelerate if AI removes bottlenecks, but does not predict diffusion will be much faster than previous technologies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different speeds here. One is the speed at which the technology gets better, and the other is the speed at which organizations can actually absorb it. Those aren’t necessarily the same.

Coding is a good example of where adoption can move very quickly. You have people who understand the technology, they can try it themselves, and they can often tell pretty quickly whether it’s helping. But in other parts of the economy, you need to change workflows, connect the model to internal systems, and figure out how to evaluate whether it’s doing the job reliably. That takes longer, even if the underlying capability is already there.

So I’d expect adoption to be uneven. You’ll see very rapid growth in particular tasks and industries, alongside places where it feels surprisingly slow. Our revenue growth is evidence that there’s real demand, but I wouldn’t extrapolate directly from that to say the entire economy transforms at the same rate. The interesting question is how quickly those early uses turn into broader changes in how organizations operate.

r001.rationale: The response says organizations must change workflows, connect models to internal systems, and evaluate reliability, which slows adoption even when the capability is already there.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the pace at which the technology improves from how quickly organizations can absorb it and adoption spreads.

r003.rationale: The response predicts uneven adoption, with some uses moving quickly and broader changes taking longer, but does not compare diffusion speed with previous technologies.
